about.title: About RAFEEQ
about.heroTitle: Making genetic information easier to understand, while keeping people in control.
about.heroIntro: RAFEEQ was designed around a simple idea: people deserve to understand their genetic health information without being judged, pressured, or overwhelmed.

purpose.heading: Why RAFEEQ exists
purpose.body:
Genetic screening can help identify inherited health risks, but a test result alone does not guarantee understanding.

Individuals and couples may receive complex information without knowing what carrier status means, how inheritance works or what questions to ask next.

These challenges can be more significant in communities where consanguineous marriage is practised and where conversations about inherited conditions may involve family, cultural and personal considerations.

RAFEEQ addresses this gap by connecting genetic education, understandable screening information, privacy-conscious sharing and counselling navigation in one accessible platform.

mission.heading: Our mission
mission.body: To make inherited health information understandable and accessible so individuals and families can explore potential risks and seek appropriate professional guidance with confidence.

vision.heading: Our vision
vision.body: A future in which every person can access clear, respectful and reliable information about inherited health risks and make informed decisions without stigma or pressure.

people.title: People before data
people.body: We recognise that genetic information is personal and may affect entire families. Communication must be sensitive, respectful and understandable.

understanding.title: Understanding before decisions
understanding.body: We believe people need clear explanations before they can make meaningful decisions about their health.

judgement.title: Guidance without judgement
judgement.body: We do not promote or oppose any marriage or family-planning choice. We support access to information and professional counselling.

privacy.title: Privacy through responsibility
privacy.body: Genetic information deserves careful handling, meaningful consent and appropriate access controls.

approach.heading: Our approach
approach.step3: Explanations of relevant couple-level inherited risk.

commitment.heading: Our commitment
commitment.body:
We aim to make complex health information easier to understand while recognising the limits of technology.

RAFEEQ does not diagnose inherited conditions, guarantee outcomes or replace qualified healthcare professionals.

story: Genetic screening can reveal important information about inherited conditions. However, the meaning of an individual finding and its potential implications for a couple may be difficult to understand without clear communication and appropriate professional support.
RAFEEQ brings education, consent-based information sharing, understandable risk explanations, and pathways to genetic counselling into one experience.
Our approach respects personal values, family relationships, cultural context, and individual privacy.

howItWorks.title: How It Works
howItWorks.heroTitle: From screening information to informed, supported decisions.
howItWorks.heroIntro: RAFEEQ follows six stages. You decide how far to go, and nothing is shared unless you choose to share it.

step1.heading: Step 1 — Start with understanding
step1.bullet4: The purpose and limitations of screening.

step2.heading: Step 2 — Review screening information
step2.intro: Where supported information is available, RAFEEQ helps explain:
step2.bullet2: What carrier status does and does not indicate.
step2.bullet3: Which questions may require clinical interpretation.
step2.bullet4: Why additional testing or professional advice may be appropriate.

step3.heading: Step 3 — Explore couple-level considerations
step3.body:
Some inherited conditions depend on the genetic contributions of both biological parents.

For example, when both biological parents carry relevant disease-associated variants in the same autosomal recessive condition, there may be a chance of an affected child in each pregnancy.

The actual risk must be interpreted using the specific condition, variants and clinical evidence.

RAFEEQ helps explain this concept without treating every condition or couple as the same.

distinction.heading: Important distinction
distinction.body:
A carrier result is not automatically a diagnosis. A potential inherited risk is not a prediction that a child will definitely have a condition.

Clinical interpretation should be provided by qualified professionals.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.intro: Answers to common questions about RAFEEQ, genetic information, privacy and counselling.

items.a: RAFEEQ is an educational and decision-support platform that helps people understand inherited disease risk, explore screening information, and find pathways to genetic counselling.

items.q: Is RAFEEQ a genetic testing laboratory?
items.a: No. RAFEEQ does not perform laboratory genetic testing. It is designed to support understanding and access to appropriate guidance.
Individuals and couples who want to understand inherited conditions, screening concepts, and possible next steps.
A carrier has a genetic variant associated with a particular inherited condition. For many recessive conditions, carriers do not have the condition themselves.

items.q: Does being a carrier mean my child will have the condition?
items.a: No. A carrier finding alone does not establish that a future child will have an inherited condition. Risk depends on the relevant findings from both biological parents, the gene, variants, and inheritance pattern.

items.q: Does consanguineous marriage mean a child will have an inherited condition?
items.a: No. A biological relationship between partners does not establish that a child will have a particular inherited condition. Appropriate screening and professional interpretation can help clarify relevant risks.
No. RAFEEQ provides educational explanations and decision support. Diagnosis and clinical interpretation require appropriate clinical assessment.

items.q: Can my partner automatically see my screening results?
items.a: No. Personal results are private by default. Sharing requires your explicit permission.

items.q: Can my family access my information?
items.a: No. Family members do not receive access automatically.
Yes. You can revoke future access to information you previously chose to share. Revoking cannot undo information that has already been viewed or independently kept by the other person.

items.q: When should I speak to a genetics professional?
items.a: Professional guidance may be important when findings are complex, inconclusive, potentially high-impact, or require clinical interpretation.

items.q: Does RAFEEQ recommend whether people should marry?
items.a: No. RAFEEQ does not recommend or discourage marriage. It supports understanding, personal autonomy, and informed decision-making.
No. It can provide educational information about pathways and options, but it does not provide treatment or replace professional care.

privacyPolicy.title: Privacy Policy
privacyPolicy.intro: RAFEEQ recognises that genetic and family health information is personal. We aim to handle information responsibly, explain its intended use and support meaningful consent.

collect.heading: 1. Information we may process
collect.body:
Depending on the features used, information may include basic account or profile information; information voluntarily entered by a user; genetic screening information provided by a user; information related to consent and sharing preferences; and technical information necessary to operate the service.

In the demo, language, theme and reading-mode preferences may be stored in your browser. Demo sessions use temporary in-browser state and fictional example profiles.

use.heading: 2. How information is used
use.body:
Information may be used to provide requested platform features, explain educational content, support relevant workflows and improve service functionality.

RAFEEQ must not use sensitive genetic information for unrelated purposes without an appropriate lawful basis and required consent.

consent.heading: 3. Consent and sharing
consent.body:
Genetic information may reveal details relevant to biological relatives as well as the person tested. Sharing should therefore be carefully considered. Users should understand what information is being shared, with whom and for what purpose before using a sharing feature.

In the couple privacy screens, separate sharing scopes are modelled (e.g. overlap with partner, sharing with clinic). Revocation is immediate in the demo UI and logged in the audit timeline.

access.heading: 4. Access and permissions
access.body: Access depends on user roles, permissions and the features in use. In the demo, couple, counsellor, analyst and admin areas are separated by role. Being a partner, family member or healthcare professional does not by itself give someone access to another person's results.

minimise.heading: 5. Data minimisation
minimise.body: RAFEEQ aims to collect and process only information needed to provide the requested functionality.

storage.heading: 6. Storage and security
storage.body: Information security depends on the systems and safeguards in use. This policy is not a guarantee of encryption, secure hosting or regulatory certification. The demo runs in your browser with example data.

retention.heading: 7. Retention and deletion
retention.body: Retention periods and deletion procedures will be defined for the live service in line with applicable legal requirements. In the demo, session data stays in your browser and can be reset at any time.

thirdParty.heading: 8. Third-party services
thirdParty.body: Fonts are self-hosted. Any external service that processes user information will be identified in this policy.

rights.heading: 9. Your choices and rights
rights.body: Users will be informed of the available rights and procedures for access, correction, consent withdrawal and deletion, subject to applicable law. Questions can be sent to help@rafeeq.health.

contact.heading: 10. Contact
contact.body: A verified privacy contact and organisation identity must be added before publication.

risk.title: Understanding Genetic Risk
risk.heroTitle: Understanding genetic risk, clearly and without judgement.
risk.heroIntro: Carrier status, inheritance patterns and couple-level risk are easy to confuse. This page explains each one in plain language.

carrier.heading: What does being a carrier mean?
carrier.body: A carrier has a genetic variant associated with a particular inherited condition. In many recessive conditions, carriers do not have the condition themselves. However, if both biological parents carry relevant disease-associated variants in the same gene, there may be a chance that a child inherits the condition.
carrier.note: Being a carrier does not automatically mean that a person is ill or that their future children will have an inherited condition.

couple.heading: Why one result is not enough to determine a couple's risk.
couple.body: An individual screening result provides information about that individual. Estimating potential risk for a child generally requires consideration of both biological parents' relevant findings, the specific gene and variants involved, the inheritance pattern, and clinical interpretation.

risk.patternsIntro: Inheritance patterns differ, and not every inherited condition follows the same model.

patterns.title: Autosomal recessive
patterns.body: A child is generally affected only when they inherit a relevant variant in the same gene from each biological parent. People with one variant are usually carriers.

patterns.title: Autosomal dominant
patterns.body: One copy of a relevant variant can be enough to cause a condition. A person with the variant may pass it on, and effects can vary between people.

patterns.title: X-linked
patterns.body: The relevant gene is on the X chromosome. Because of this, the chance and the effects can differ between male and female children.

example.heading: Example: autosomal recessive inheritance
example.intro: When both biological parents carry relevant pathogenic variants in the same gene associated with an autosomal recessive condition, a typical model for each pregnancy is:

outcomes.label: chance of a child who is a carrier
chance of a child who inherits neither familial variant

example.caveat: This example applies only to the relevant autosomal recessive situation. It is not a universal risk estimate for every couple or every inherited condition. Each pregnancy is an independent event.

family.heading: Understanding family relationships and inherited risk without judgement.
body: Biological relatives may have a higher chance of sharing certain inherited variants because they have common ancestors. However, a family relationship alone does not establish that a child will inherit a particular condition.
Individual and couple-level screening information, family history, and appropriate professional interpretation are important.

diagnosis.heading: Risk is not diagnosis
diagnosis.body: A calculated or estimated risk is not the same as a diagnosis. Screening can identify findings that may need further assessment, but it cannot always establish whether a person or future child has a condition.

next.heading: After screening: confirmatory assessment and options
items: Screening and diagnosis are different. Some findings need confirmatory assessment before any conclusion is drawn.
Ambiguous or inconclusive results should be interpreted by a qualified professional.
Genetic counselling can help you understand findings, uncertainty and available options.

Options may include further testing, specialist consultation and reproductive-genomics services where available. Which options are appropriate depends on individual circumstances, clinical context, availability and personal values.
next.note: RAFEEQ does not recommend any particular reproductive decision and does not claim that a specific service is available at any institution.

conditions.title: Inherited Conditions
conditions.heroTitle: Inherited conditions, explained in plain language.
conditions.heroIntro: A short educational guide to some inherited conditions that are often discussed in screening programmes.

labels.advice: When professional advice may be needed

items.name: Beta-thalassemia
items.summary: Beta-thalassemia is an inherited blood disorder affecting hemoglobin production. Some people carry a variant without having the severe form of the condition. If both biological parents carry relevant pathogenic variants in the HBB gene, their children may have an increased chance of inheriting a clinically significant form.
items.carrier: A carrier usually does not have the severe form, though some carriers have mild changes in blood tests.
items.screening: Blood tests and genetic screening can identify carrier status before decisions about having children.
items.advice: When both partners have relevant findings, or when a blood test or genetic result is unclear.

items.name: Sickle cell disease
items.summary: Sickle cell disease is an inherited blood disorder involving hemoglobin. The implications of carrier findings depend on the variants inherited from both biological parents.
items.carrier: Carriers (sometimes called sickle cell trait) usually do not have sickle cell disease.
items.screening: Screening can show which hemoglobin variants each partner carries, which matters for how variants may combine.
items.advice: When both partners carry relevant hemoglobin variants, including different variants that can combine.

items.name: Spinal muscular atrophy
items.summary: Spinal muscular atrophy is a genetic condition affecting motor neurons and muscle function. Many forms are associated with changes in the SMN1 gene. Screening and interpretation can involve technical limitations and residual risk.
items.pattern: Most forms are autosomal recessive (SMN1 gene).
items.carrier: Carriers usually have no symptoms. Some carrier arrangements are hard to detect with standard tests.
items.screening: Carrier screening can estimate SMN1 copy number, but results can have technical limitations.
items.advice: When a result is inconclusive or reports residual risk, or when there is a family history.

items.name: Cystic fibrosis
items.summary: Cystic fibrosis is an inherited condition associated with variants in the CFTR gene. Carrier findings require consideration of both biological parents' relevant variants.
items.carrier: Carriers usually do not have cystic fibrosis.
items.screening: Panels test for selected CFTR variants. Which variants are included differs between panels.
items.advice: When one or both partners have a CFTR finding, or when a panel does not cover variants common in your family background.

conditions.disclaimer: These descriptions are general educational information. They do not establish a diagnosis or provide an individualised risk assessment. Screening panels differ, and not every panel includes every condition.
